## Linear Covariance Propagation

Lets look into how linear covariance propagation works and the benefits of using it. In state estimation, two important quantities are the 
mean, $\mathbf{x}$, and the covariance, $\mathbf{P}$. The covariance represents the uncertainty in the state estimate. Imagine a bell curve, representing a 1-dimensional distribution; the 
covariance would represent how "wide" the bell curve is, where a larger covariance corelates to a "wider" bell curve.

With this in mind, lets look at a scenario involving two satellites in formation flight. Let's call the satellite being followed the "Chief" and the following satellite the "Deputy". In this 
scenario we will assume the state of the Chief satellite is perfectly known, while the Deputy has some covariance associated with its state estimate. 

![Chief-Deputy formation flight geometry. *Diagram generated with Gemini.*](images/formation_flight.jpg){#fig-formation width="80%" fig-align="center"}

As the two satellites progress in their orbits, the covariance can also be propagated forward to show the uncertainty in the deputies state over time using linear covariance propagation. 
@eq-lincov is the equation used for performing this propagation.

$$
\mathbf{P}(t) = \mathbf{\Phi}(t,t_0) \mathbf{P}_0 \mathbf{\Phi}(t,t_0)^T + \mathbf{Q} 
$${#eq-lincov}

In this equation $\mathbf{\Phi}$ represents the state transition matrix, which uses linearized dynamics to propagate the covariance from $t_0$ to $t$. 
$Q$ represents process noise to account for unmodeled perturbations, though in our scenario this will be zero because we will be modeling the system using two-body equations of motion with no perturbations.
 @eq-lincov will do a good job at propagating the covariance given that the uncertainty remains gaussian and that the linearized dynamics contained 
 in $\mathbf{\Phi}$ accurately represents the true system dynamics.
